meta.subtitle: A topic-and-flow map of introductory electromagnetic field theory
meta.text: Sadiku, Elements of Electromagnetics, 6th ed. (section numbers are suggested reading, not required)

edgeKinds.requires: You need the source topic before the target topic makes sense.
edgeKinds.translates: Integral and differential forms of the same law, converted by a theorem.
edgeKinds.mirrors: The electrostatic / magnetostatic twin of a topic.

maxwell.title: Maxwell's equations for static fields
maxwell.caption: Four laws, one grid. Rows: which field. Columns: what question you ask of it. Each cell has an integral form and a differential form; the theorem at the top of the column converts between them. In statics the two rows never talk to each other except through the Lorentz force — the two cells that equal zero are where time variation will later couple them.

columns.label: How does the field spread out?  (divergence · flux)
How does the field circulate?  (curl · circulation)

nodes.name: Vectors, dot & cross products
nodes.summary: Components, unit vectors, addition and subtraction, projections, and the two products. The cross product gives the direction of magnetic forces; the dot product gives flux and work.
pitfalls: Treating the cross product as commutative. **A** × **B** = −**B** × **A**; the order sets the sign, and the sign is a direction.
Forgetting that a unit vector in cylindrical or spherical coordinates (â_ρ, â_φ, â_r, â_θ) changes direction from point to point. Only â_x, â_y, â_z are constant.

check.q: What is â_x × â_y, and what is â_y × â_x?
check.a: â_z and −â_z. The cross product is anticommutative; the order sets the sign.

nodes.name: Coordinate systems & constant surfaces
nodes.summary: Cartesian, cylindrical and spherical coordinates, how to transform between them, and the surfaces where one coordinate is held constant. Picking the coordinate system that matches the symmetry of a problem is most of the work in Gauss's and Ampère's laws.
nodes.equation: d\mathbf{l},\; d\mathbf{S},\; dv \text{ in Cartesian, cylindrical and spherical coordinates}
pitfalls: Mixing up which coordinate is held constant on a surface. ρ = const is a cylinder; z = const is a plane; r = const is a sphere; θ = const is a cone.
Using the wrong differential element. In spherical coordinates the surface element on a sphere is r² sin θ dθ dφ, not dθ dφ.

check.q: In spherical coordinates, what shape is the surface θ = π/2?
check.a: The xy-plane. θ is measured from the +z axis, so θ = π/2 is everything at 90° from it.

nodes.name: Line, surface & volume integrals
nodes.summary: Integrating a scalar or vector quantity along a path, over a surface, or through a volume. Every continuous charge or current distribution, every flux, and every circulation is one of these integrals.
pitfalls: Pulling a vector out of an integral when its *direction* varies along the path or surface. Only magnitude-and-direction-constant quantities come out.
Losing track of what the integration variable is. For a line charge, integrate along the charge, not along the field point.

check.q: A line charge ρ_L runs along the z-axis from z = 0 to z = L. Write the total charge as an integral.
check.a: Q = ∫₀ᴸ ρ_L dz. If ρ_L is constant this is just ρ_L L.

nodes.name: Flux — "how much passes through"
nodes.summary: The surface integral of a vector field: how much of the field pokes through a surface. Flux is the physical meaning of the whole left column of Maxwell's equations. Read divergence as 'flux per unit volume'.
pitfalls: Counting flux through a closed surface as 'total field present.' Field lines that go in and come back out contribute zero net flux.

check.q: A uniform field E points along +z. What is the flux through a flat disk lying in the xy-plane, and through the same disk tilted 60° from the xy-plane?
check.a: Ψ = E·A for the flat disk; Ψ = E·A·cos 60° = ½ E·A when tilted. Flux counts only the component of E normal to the surface.

nodes.name: Circulation — "how much goes around"
nodes.summary: The closed line integral of a vector field: how much the field pushes you along a loop. Circulation is the physical meaning of the right column of Maxwell's equations. Read curl as 'circulation per unit area'.
pitfalls: Thinking a field with curved field lines must have circulation. A field can curve and still have zero circulation around every loop — the static E field does exactly that.

check.q: Is the circulation of a static electric field around a closed loop ever nonzero?
check.a: No — ∮E·dl = 0 for any loop in electrostatics. Nonzero circulation of E requires a time-varying magnetic field.

nodes.name: Gradient
nodes.summary: The direction and rate of steepest increase of a scalar field. Gradient never appears in Maxwell's equations directly; it is how you climb back from a potential to a field.
pitfalls: Mixing up the direction. ∇V points toward *increasing* V; E = −∇V points downhill, from high potential to low.
Applying the Cartesian formula in cylindrical or spherical coordinates. The φ and θ components pick up 1/ρ or 1/r factors.

check.q: V increases toward +x. Which way does E point?
check.a: Toward −x. E = −∇V points from high potential to low, opposite to the gradient.

nodes.name: Divergence
nodes.summary: Net outward flux per unit volume at a point. Positive where field lines start, negative where they end, zero where they just pass through.
pitfalls: Reading 'the field lines spread out here' as positive divergence. Lines spreading while weakening can have zero divergence — the point-charge field does, everywhere except at the charge.

check.q: What is ∇·E at a point in empty space 1 m from a point charge?
check.a: Zero. Divergence is nonzero only where charge density is nonzero; at that point ρ = 0.

nodes.name: Curl
nodes.summary: Circulation per unit area at a point, as a vector along the axis of rotation. A field with zero curl everywhere is conservative and has a scalar potential.
pitfalls: Expecting curl to be a scalar. It is a vector; its direction is the axis the field circulates around, by the right-hand rule.
Treating zero curl as 'the field is uniform.' Zero curl means conservative, not constant.

check.q: Which has nonzero curl: a uniform field, or the field B that circles a straight wire, evaluated outside the wire?
check.a: Neither. The uniform field has zero curl trivially; the field outside a wire circles but its curl is zero because no current flows there. Curl measures local circulation, not whether lines curve.

nodes.name: Divergence theorem
nodes.summary: Total flux out of a closed surface equals the volume integral of the divergence inside it. This is the translator between the integral and differential forms of Gauss's law and of ∇·B = 0.
pitfalls: Applying it to an open surface. The theorem needs a *closed* surface and the volume it encloses.
Forgetting it is pure mathematics. It says nothing about physics until you put Gauss's law into it.

check.q: The divergence theorem relates which two things?
check.a: The net flux of a vector field out of a closed surface, and the volume integral of its divergence over the enclosed region.

nodes.name: Stokes' theorem
nodes.summary: Circulation around a closed loop equals the flux of the curl through any surface bounded by the loop. This is the translator between the integral and differential forms of Ampère's law and of ∇×E = 0.
pitfalls: Thinking the surface is fixed. Any surface bounded by the loop works — so pick the easiest one.
Getting the orientation wrong. The loop direction and the surface normal are tied together by the right-hand rule.

check.q: Stokes' theorem relates which two things?
check.a: The circulation of a vector field around a closed loop, and the flux of its curl through any surface bounded by that loop.

nodes.name: Charge distributions
nodes.summary: Discrete point charges, and line, surface and volume charge densities. Charge is the source of the electric field; a continuous distribution is handled by integrating over infinitesimal point charges.
pitfalls: Mixing up the charge densities. ρ_L is per length, ρ_S per area, ρ_v per volume; the integral that gives total charge must match.
Treating a 'point charge' as physically tiny. It is a model: anything whose size is small compared with the distance you care about.

check.q: A uniformly charged spherical shell of radius a carries total charge Q. What is its surface charge density?
check.a: ρ_S = Q / (4πa²).

nodes.name: Coulomb's law
nodes.summary: The force between two point charges, from Coulomb's torsion-balance experiment. Dividing out the test charge defines the electric field. The explicit solution to the 'divergence' half of electrostatics.

resources.label: oPhysics · Coulomb forces on three charges

pitfalls: Dropping the vector. Coulomb's law gives a direction along the line joining the charges; summing magnitudes alone is wrong unless everything is collinear.
Using the distance to the wrong point. R is from the *source* charge to the *field* point, and â_R points the same way.

check.q: Two equal charges are 1 m apart. If the distance is doubled, by what factor does the force change?
check.a: It drops to one quarter. Coulomb force goes as 1/R².

nodes.name: The electric field E
nodes.summary: Force per unit charge on a test charge. Fields of discrete charges add as vectors; fields of continuous distributions are integrals of Coulomb's law. Field lines start on positive charge and end on negative charge.
pitfalls: Thinking the field exists only where there is a test charge. E is defined at every point in space whether or not anything is there to feel it.
Summing the fields of a continuous distribution without splitting them into components first. Each dQ contributes a vector; integrate component by component.

check.q: Two equal positive charges sit at x = −a and x = +a. What is E at the origin?
check.a: Zero. The two fields are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so they cancel.

nodes.name: The electric dipole
nodes.summary: Two equal and opposite charges a small distance apart. Its field falls off as 1/r³, and it is the building block for polarization in dielectrics.
pitfalls: Expecting the dipole field to fall off as 1/r². The two charges nearly cancel at a distance, so the leading term goes as 1/r³.
Using the far-field dipole formula close to the charges, where it is not valid.

check.q: Along the dipole axis, how does the electric field magnitude scale with distance r far from the dipole?
check.a: As 1/r³ — one power faster than a single charge, because the two charges nearly cancel.

nodes.name: Gauss's law (integral)
nodes.summary: The total electric flux out of any closed surface equals the enclosed charge over ε₀. Maxwell's first equation in the form you can compute with: pick a surface that matches the symmetry and the integral collapses.

check.q: A point charge sits just *outside* a closed surface. What is the net electric flux through the surface?
check.a: Zero. Every field line that enters the surface also leaves it, so the net flux is zero even though E is nonzero on the surface. Only enclosed charge produces net flux.

pitfalls: Treating Gauss's law as a formula for E. It is a statement about total flux; it only yields E when symmetry lets you pull |E| out of the integral.
Counting charge outside the surface in Q_enc. Outside charge shapes E on the surface but contributes zero *net* flux.

tryIt.label: Equation builder: choose the symmetry, surface and collapsed form step by step

nodes.name: Gauss's law (differential)
nodes.summary: The divergence of E at a point equals the charge density there over ε₀. Same law as the integral form, translated by the divergence theorem. This is the form that leads to Poisson's equation.
pitfalls: Expecting ∇·E to be nonzero wherever the field is strong. It is nonzero only *where the charge is*. In empty space ∇·E = 0 no matter how big E is.

check.q: Starting from ∮E·dS = Q_enc/ε₀, which theorem gets you to ∇·E = ρ_v/ε₀?
check.a: The divergence theorem, which turns the closed-surface flux into ∫(∇·E)dv; equating integrands with Q_enc = ∫ρ_v dv gives the differential form.

nodes.name: Applying Gauss: symmetry & composite structures
nodes.summary: Spheres, infinite lines and planes, coaxial cables, nested shells. The recipe: identify the symmetry, choose the matching Gaussian surface, pull |E| out of the integral, solve region by region.
pitfalls: Using Gauss's law where there is no symmetry. The law is always true; it is only *useful* when |E| is constant on the surface you chose.
Forgetting that Q_enc is only the charge inside the surface — outside charge still contributes to E, but its net flux through the surface is zero.

check.q: Why can't you use Gauss's law alone to find E from an electric dipole?
check.a: There is no surface on which |E| is constant and E is everywhere parallel or perpendicular to the surface. Gauss's law still holds — it just doesn't let you pull E out of the integral.

tryIt.label: Equation builder: choose the symmetry, surface and collapsed form step by step

nodes.name: E is conservative:  ∮ E·dl = 0
nodes.summary: The work done moving a charge around any closed loop in a static electric field is zero, so the work between two points is path-independent. This is what makes a scalar potential possible.

check.q: What property of E lets us define a potential at all?
check.a: Its circulation around any closed path is zero (∇×E = 0), so the work between two points is independent of path and a single-valued scalar V can be assigned to each point.

pitfalls: Confusing 'the integral around a closed loop is zero' with 'the integral along any path is zero.' Only the closed-loop integral vanishes; an open path gives the potential difference.

tryIt.label: Equation builder: route, reference point and path for V, step by step

nodes.name: ∇×E = 0
nodes.summary: The static electric field has no curl anywhere. Translated from the integral form by Stokes' theorem. This cell of Maxwell's equations is where Faraday's law appears once fields vary in time.
pitfalls: Reading ∇×E = 0 as 'E has no rotation in the picture.' It is a local statement at each point; field lines can still curve.

check.q: What does ∇×E = 0 let you define?
check.a: A scalar potential V with E = −∇V. Any curl-free field is the gradient of something.

nodes.name: Electric potential V
nodes.summary: Work per unit charge to bring a test charge in from a reference point. A scalar, so it adds as a number rather than a vector. E is the negative gradient of V; V is the negative line integral of E.

resources.label: oPhysics · Charged particle in an electric field

pitfalls: Dropping the minus sign in E = −∇V, or in V = −∫E·dl.
Treating V as a vector. Potentials of several charges add as plain numbers — that is the whole reason to use them.

check.q: The potential in a region is V = 3x² (volts, x in meters). What is E at x = 1 m?
check.a: E = −∇V = −6x â_x, so at x = 1 m, E = −6 â_x V/m. It points toward decreasing x, i.e. downhill in V.

tryIt.label: Equation builder: route, reference point and path for V, step by step

nodes.name: Energy in charge distributions & in the field
nodes.summary: The work to assemble a set of charges, which can be rewritten as an energy density stored in the field itself. The field-energy form is what you use for capacitors.
pitfalls: Double counting. The ½ in ½∫ρV dv is there because each pair of charges would otherwise be counted twice.
Expecting the two energy formulas to disagree. ½∫ρV dv and ½∫ε₀E² dv give the same total for any complete distribution; they just place the energy in different places.

check.q: Three equal charges are assembled from infinity into a triangle. How many pair interactions contribute to the stored energy?
check.a: Three — one for each pair. The ½∫ρV dv formula counts each pair once because of the ½.

nodes.name: Poisson's & Laplace's equations
nodes.summary: Substitute E = −∇V into ∇·E = ρ/ε₀ and you get one scalar equation for V. With no charge in the region it becomes Laplace's equation. Solving these with boundary conditions is the general method of electrostatics.
pitfalls: Using Laplace's equation in a region that contains charge. Laplace is the special case ρ = 0; with charge present you need Poisson.
Forgetting boundary conditions. The equation alone has infinitely many solutions; the boundary values pick the one you want.

check.q: Between the plates of a charged parallel-plate capacitor (vacuum, no charge between the plates), which equation does V satisfy?
check.a: Laplace's equation, ∇²V = 0 — there is no charge density in the gap. The plates enter as boundary conditions.

nodes.name: Numerical methods: mesh grids & iterative solvers
nodes.summary: Discretize space onto a grid, replace derivatives with differences, and iterate until the potential stops changing. Accuracy versus runtime is the trade-off; this is what field simulation software does under the hood.
pitfalls: Trusting a result because it converged. A converged iteration can still be wrong if the grid is too coarse or a boundary was set up badly — compare with an analytical case first.
Making the grid finer than you need. Runtime grows fast with grid size; refine until the answer stops changing, then stop.

check.q: In the iterative Laplace solver, what does the update V_ij ← ¼(sum of four neighbors) enforce?
check.a: That the discrete second derivatives in x and y sum to zero — the finite-difference version of ∇²V = 0. Repeating it drives the grid toward the solution.

nodes.name: Conductors: induced charge, current, resistance
nodes.summary: Inside a perfect conductor in equilibrium E is zero and the surface is an equipotential; charge rearranges on the surface to make it so. With a steady current, Ohm's law in field form gives the resistance of a structure.
pitfalls: Assuming E = 0 inside a conductor that is carrying a current. The zero-field result holds only in *electrostatic* equilibrium.
Putting charge inside a conductor. In equilibrium all excess charge sits on the surface.

check.q: A hollow conducting sphere has charge +Q placed at its center. What charge appears on the inner and outer surfaces?
check.a: −Q on the inner surface (so E = 0 inside the metal) and +Q on the outer surface (the conductor is neutral overall).

nodes.name: Polarization P & bound charge
nodes.summary: An applied field stretches or aligns the molecular dipoles in a dielectric. The net effect is equivalent to bound surface and volume charge, which partially cancels the applied field.
pitfalls: Thinking bound charge is 'fake.' It is real charge, just not free to move; it produces real fields.
Expecting polarization to add to the applied field. Inside a dielectric the bound charge *reduces* the net field.

check.q: A dielectric slab is placed in a uniform field E₀. Is the field inside the slab larger or smaller than E₀?
check.a: Smaller. Bound surface charge produces a field opposing E₀, so the net field inside is E₀/ε_r for a linear dielectric.

nodes.name: Displacement field D & permittivity
nodes.summary: Define D so that its flux depends only on the free charge you control, hiding the bound charge. In a linear dielectric D is just ε times E. Gauss's law in a dielectric is Gauss's law with D and free charge.
pitfalls: Thinking D is 'the real field' in a dielectric. E is what exerts force; D is bookkeeping that hides the bound charge so Gauss's law only needs the free charge.

check.q: A parallel-plate capacitor has a fixed charge on its plates. A dielectric slab is inserted. What happens to D and to E between the plates?
check.a: D stays the same (it depends only on the free charge). E drops by a factor of ε_r, because the bound charge on the dielectric surfaces partially cancels the plate charge.

nodes.name: Boundary conditions for E and D
nodes.summary: At an interface, tangential E is continuous and the jump in normal D equals the surface charge. Both follow directly from the integral forms: a tiny loop for the tangential condition, a tiny pillbox for the normal one.
pitfalls: Applying the tangential condition to D or the normal condition to E. Tangential: E is continuous. Normal: D jumps by the free surface charge.

check.q: At the surface of a perfect conductor in electrostatics, what are the tangential E and normal D just outside?
check.a: Tangential E is zero (it must match the zero field inside) and normal D equals the surface charge density ρ_s.

nodes.name: Capacitance, stored energy, fringe fields
nodes.summary: Charge stored per volt between two conductors, a property of the geometry and the dielectric only. Compute it from Q/V or from the stored energy. Real capacitors have fringe fields at the edges that the ideal formulas ignore.
pitfalls: Thinking capacitance depends on the charge or voltage. It depends only on geometry and the dielectric; Q/V is the same at any Q.
Using the parallel-plate formula for plates that are not close together compared with their size. Fringe fields make the real C larger.

check.q: A parallel-plate capacitor's plate separation is halved. What happens to C?
check.a: It doubles. C = εA/d for close plates, so halving d doubles C.

nodes.name: Current distributions
nodes.summary: Line currents, surface current density K and volume current density J. Moving charge is the source of the magnetic field, in the same way static charge is the source of the electric field.
pitfalls: Confusing I, K and J. I is a total in amperes; K is amperes per meter across a surface; J is amperes per square meter through a surface.
Forgetting that steady currents must flow in closed loops. There is no such thing as a static isolated current segment.

check.q: A surface current K = 5 â_x A/m flows on the z = 0 plane. How much current crosses a 2 m segment of the y-axis?
check.a: 10 A. Surface current density times the width perpendicular to the flow.

nodes.name: Biot–Savart law
nodes.summary: The magnetic field of a current element, from Ampère's and Biot and Savart's experiments. It plays the role Coulomb's law plays in electrostatics: the explicit solution you integrate over the source.
pitfalls: Putting the vector dl × â_R in the wrong order. Swapping them flips the sign of B.

check.q: A current element I dl points along +z at the origin. What is dB at a point on the +x axis?
check.a: Along +y: dl × â_R = â_z × â_x = â_y. The field circles the current.

nodes.name: The magnetic field B
nodes.summary: Fields of straight wires, loops and solenoids come from integrating Biot–Savart. Field lines of B always close on themselves; they never start or end anywhere.
pitfalls: Reading the direction of B as 'along the current.' B circles the current; use the right-hand rule with your thumb along I.
Expecting B to point from north to south in a magnet the way E points from + to −. Field lines of B close on themselves; they do not start or end.

check.q: At the center of a circular current loop, which way does B point relative to the current direction?
check.a: Along the loop axis, by the right-hand rule — curl your fingers with the current and your thumb gives B.

nodes.name: Lorentz force
nodes.summary: The force on a moving charge in electric and magnetic fields. The only equation in this course containing both E and B, and so the one place the two halves of the map touch directly.

resources.label: oPhysics · Charged particle in a magnetic field

pitfalls: Getting the direction of u × B backwards. Right-hand rule: fingers along u, curl toward B, thumb is the force on a positive charge — flip it for a negative one.
Expecting the magnetic force to do work. It is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it only changes direction.

check.q: A proton moves along +x through a magnetic field along +y. Which way is the force?
check.a: +z. F = q u × B, and x̂ × ŷ = ẑ for a positive charge.

nodes.name: Forces between currents; torque & moment
nodes.summary: Sum the Lorentz force over the charges in a wire and you get the force on a current element in a field, then the force between two wires. A current loop in a field feels a torque, which defines its magnetic dipole moment.
pitfalls: Expecting the force on a current element to be along the current. It is perpendicular to both the current and the field.
Remembering 'parallel currents attract' but not why. Each wire sits in the other's circling field; apply dF = I dl × B to see the direction.

check.q: Two long parallel wires carry currents in opposite directions. Do they attract or repel?
check.a: Repel. Antiparallel currents repel; parallel currents attract.

nodes.name: Ampère's law (integral)
nodes.summary: The circulation of B around any closed loop equals μ₀ times the current threading the loop. The magnetostatic counterpart of Gauss's law: with the right symmetry the integral collapses and B falls out.

check.q: Is Ampère's law ∮B·dl = μ₀I_enc valid for a short straight wire segment carrying current I?
check.a: The law as written assumes steady currents, which must form closed circuits. A finite segment alone is not a steady current; you need Biot–Savart (or the full time-varying law) for it.

pitfalls: Treating Ampère's law as a formula for B. Like Gauss's law it is a statement about a total — the circulation — and only yields B when symmetry lets you pull |B| out.
Forgetting the sign convention: the direction you traverse the loop and the direction that counts as positive current are linked by the right-hand rule.

tryIt.label: Equation builder: choose the symmetry, loop and collapsed form step by step

nodes.name: ∇×B = μ₀J
nodes.summary: The curl of B at a point is μ₀ times the current density there. Translated from the integral form by Stokes' theorem. In time-varying fields a displacement-current term joins J here.
pitfalls: Expecting ∇×B to be nonzero wherever B is strong. It is nonzero only where current actually flows. Outside a wire the curl is zero even though B is not.

check.q: Inside a wire carrying uniform current density J, what is ∇×B?
check.a: μ₀J, pointing along the current. Outside the wire it is zero.

nodes.name: Applying Ampère: symmetry & composite structures
nodes.summary: Infinite wires, coaxial cables, solenoids, toroids, current sheets. Same recipe as Gauss: find the symmetry, pick the Amperian loop that follows it, pull |B| out, solve region by region.
pitfalls: Choosing an Amperian loop that doesn't follow a field line. If |B| isn't constant along the loop, the integral won't collapse.
Counting a current that passes beside the loop rather than through the surface it bounds.

check.q: For a long solenoid with n turns per meter carrying I, what is B inside and outside?
check.a: Inside: B = μ₀nI along the axis. Outside (ideal, infinitely long): zero. A rectangular Amperian loop straddling the winding gives both.

tryIt.label: Equation builder: choose the symmetry, loop and collapsed form step by step

nodes.name: ∮ B·dS = 0
nodes.summary: The net magnetic flux out of any closed surface is zero: there are no magnetic charges for field lines to start or end on. Flux through an open surface is still meaningful and is what inductance is built on.

check.q: Can the net magnetic flux through a closed surface ever be nonzero?
check.a: No. ∮B·dS = 0 always, because there are no magnetic charges. Field lines of B never begin or end.

pitfalls: Concluding that the flux of B through *every* surface is zero. Only closed surfaces give zero; flux through an open surface (a coil's cross-section) is what inductance is built on.

nodes.name: ∇·B = 0
nodes.summary: B has no divergence anywhere, in statics or otherwise. Translated from the integral form by the divergence theorem. Because of this, B can always be written as the curl of a vector potential.
pitfalls: Thinking ∇·B = 0 is a statics-only result. It holds always, time-varying or not; it is the one Maxwell equation that never gains a term.

check.q: Why does ∇·B = 0 guarantee a vector potential exists?
check.a: The divergence of any curl is identically zero, so a divergence-free field can always be written as the curl of some A.

nodes.name: Magnetic dipole, magnetization M & bound currents
nodes.summary: A small current loop is a magnetic dipole; a material full of aligned dipoles has a magnetization M. The net effect is equivalent to bound surface and volume currents, the magnetic twin of bound charge.
pitfalls: Treating a bar magnet as having magnetic 'charges' at its ends. The equivalent description is bound surface current circulating around the magnet.
Expecting bound currents to dissipate power. They are not conduction currents; nothing is moving through a resistance.

check.q: A uniformly magnetized cylinder has magnetization M along its axis. Where is the bound current?
check.a: Only on the curved surface, as K_b = M × â_n circling the cylinder — like a solenoid. The volume bound current J_b = ∇×M is zero because M is uniform.

nodes.name: Auxiliary field H & permeability
nodes.summary: Define H so that its circulation depends only on the free current you control, hiding the bound currents. In a linear material B is just μ times H. Ampère's law in a material is Ampère's law with H and free current.
pitfalls: Thinking H is 'the field in a material' and B is 'the field in vacuum.' Both exist everywhere; H is the bookkeeping quantity whose circulation only counts the free current.
Mixing units: B in tesla, H in amperes per meter. They are not interchangeable even in free space.

check.q: A long solenoid is filled with a linear material of relative permeability μ_r. Compared with the empty solenoid at the same current, what happens to H and to B inside?
check.a: H is unchanged (it depends only on free current: H = nI). B increases by the factor μ_r, since B = μ₀μ_r H.

nodes.name: Dia-, para- & ferromagnetism
nodes.summary: Diamagnets weakly oppose an applied field, paramagnets weakly follow it, and ferromagnets have domains that align strongly and stay aligned: saturation, hysteresis, and permanent magnets.
pitfalls: Assuming μ is a constant for ferromagnets. It depends strongly on H and on history (hysteresis); linear formulas are only approximations.
Expecting paramagnets to be noticeably magnetic. Their μ_r is barely above 1; only ferromagnets are magnetic in the everyday sense.

check.q: What does the area inside a hysteresis loop represent?
check.a: Energy lost per unit volume per cycle, dissipated as heat in the material. Transformer cores use narrow loops to keep that loss small.

nodes.name: Boundary conditions for B and H
nodes.summary: At an interface, normal B is continuous and the jump in tangential H equals the surface current. Pillbox and loop arguments again, now applied to ∮B·dS = 0 and Ampère's law.
pitfalls: Swapping the conditions. Normal B is continuous; tangential H jumps by the surface current. Compare: normal D jumps, tangential E is continuous.

check.q: At an interface with no surface current, which component of B is continuous and which component of H is continuous?
check.a: Normal B and tangential H are both continuous. Tangential B and normal H jump if the two permeabilities differ.

nodes.name: Flux linkage, self & mutual inductance
nodes.summary: Flux linked per ampere of current, a property of geometry and material only. Compute it from flux linkage or from stored energy. Real inductors have resistance, parasitic capacitance and leakage flux that the ideal formulas ignore.
pitfalls: Confusing flux Ψ with flux linkage λ = NΨ. For a coil with N turns, each turn links the flux once.

check.q: Doubling the number of turns on a long solenoid (same length, same current) does what to its inductance?
check.a: Quadruples it. B inside scales with N, and flux linkage λ = NΨ picks up another factor of N, so L ∝ N².

nodes.name: Energy in the magnetic field & in an inductor
nodes.summary: The work to establish a current against its own induced field, rewritten as an energy density stored in the field. The second route to inductance.
pitfalls: Thinking the energy is 'in the current.' It is stored in the field; the ½LI² form is just the field integral evaluated for a particular geometry.

check.q: An inductor of 2 H carries 3 A. How much energy does it store, and where is it?
check.a: W = ½LI² = 9 J, stored in the magnetic field — mostly inside the coil for a solenoid.

nodes.name: Magnetic vector potential A
nodes.summary: Because ∇·B = 0, B can be written as the curl of some vector field A. It is the magnetic twin of the scalar potential V, and it is the quantity that becomes central once fields vary in time.
pitfalls: Expecting A to be unique. Adding the gradient of any scalar to A leaves B unchanged; a choice of gauge is needed to pin it down.
Looking for a physical meaning in A's direction at a point. In magnetostatics A roughly follows the current that produces it — but only B is directly measurable here.

check.q: If A is replaced by A + ∇ψ for any scalar ψ, what happens to B?
check.a: Nothing. ∇×(∇ψ) = 0, so B = ∇×A is unchanged. This freedom is called gauge freedom.

nodes.name: Time-varying fields
nodes.summary: The two 'empty' cells of the static Maxwell equations are where the action is once things move. A changing B puts a term into ∇×E = 0 (Faraday's law); a changing E puts a term into ∇×B = μ₀J (displacement current). That coupling is what makes waves, and it is the next course.

nodes.name: Antennas & RF
nodes.summary: Everything about radiating structures is Ampère's law, boundary conditions and material properties with time dependence added. Antenna design is where this course's symmetry arguments and material models get used for real.

nodes.name: Full EM solvers
nodes.summary: The iterative Laplace solver you build on a grid is the smallest version of what finite-difference and finite-element field solvers do. Meep is a free, serious one.

nodes.name: Circuits
nodes.summary: C and L are the two field quantities that survive into circuit theory as lumped elements. Circuit simulators let you see what the stored-energy formulas do in time.

nodes.name: Fourier & signals
nodes.summary: Separable solutions of Laplace's equation are the first place Fourier series show up in field theory. From there the same mathematics runs all of signal processing and modern radio.
